Work from the project root, the main folder of the course. Read each step before you run its R chunk. All data are simulated. These exercises cannot show a finding about a real disease.

The [glossary](../docs/glossary.md) explains the course words. Each module reads its input files from disk. You do not need a saved R workspace.

```{r knit_setup, include=FALSE}
start_dir <- setwd(if (file.exists("config.R")) "." else "..")
if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = getwd())
setwd(start_dir)
```

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("R/guided.R")
cfg <- guided_init()
```

## Module 5 at a glance {#module-5-overview}

**What you will do.** You compare your study samples with a reference set of people from known world regions. You calculate a few numbers for each person that describe their genetic background. You then remove the few samples whose background is very different from the rest.

**What you will learn.**

- Why differences in [ancestry](../docs/glossary.md#ancestry) between cases and controls can create false results.
- How a [principal component](../docs/glossary.md#pca-pc) (PC) summarises genetic variation in one number per person.
- How to place study samples on reference axes and draw them in a plot.
- How to flag ancestry outliers with one fixed rule.
- How to choose and justify the number of PCs for the later analysis.

**How long it takes.** About 60 minutes. The slowest step is 5.4, which runs PLINK three times.

## 5.1 Why ancestry matters {#step-5-1}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "This supplied subset has 1,062 samples labelled EUR, AFR, EAS and SAS."} -->
### What we do

Learn how [population structure](../docs/glossary.md#population-stratification) can mislead an association study. Then look at the reference samples we will use.

### Why

Cases and controls may be recruited from groups with different ancestry. Ancestry means the broad genetic background that a person inherits from their forebears. Then the [allele frequency](../docs/glossary.md#allele-frequency) (how common an allele is in a group) can differ between cases and controls, even at sites that have nothing to do with the disease. This is called [confounding](../docs/glossary.md#confounding): a hidden factor is linked to both the group and the genetics.

A PC is a single number per person that summarises one main direction of genetic variation across many sites. Principal component analysis (PCA) is the method that finds these directions. PCA only describes patterns. Its axes are not diagnoses, nationality or ethnicity. The reference labels are background information, not a ranking of people. We define an ancestry-matched teaching cohort before we look at any association p-values.

### You need

The saved state from the end of module 4. You also need the supplied GRCh38 [reference subset](../docs/glossary.md#reference-subset), which comes with the course package.

### Command

```{r s5-1}
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
reference_samples <- guided_table(paste0(reference, ".psam"))
table(reference_samples$SuperPop)
```

## 5.2 Prepare variants for reference PCA {#step-5-2}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "48,614 shared sites are kept for the reference PCA and the projection."} -->
### What we do

Find the sites that are present in both the reference subset and the cleaned study. Only common sites on the [autosomes](../docs/glossary.md#autosome) (chromosomes 1 to 22) are used.

### Why

Nearby sites are often inherited together, so they carry the same information. This is called linkage disequilibrium ([LD](../docs/glossary.md#ld)). If PCA uses many such sites, one long correlated stretch can dominate the result. To avoid this, the supplied reference was built with [LD pruning](../docs/glossary.md#ld-pruning), which keeps one site from each correlated group. It kept only common autosomal array sites. It used an [r^2](../docs/glossary.md#r-squared) limit of 0.15 in windows of 200 kb, and it kept at most 50,000 sites.

We keep only the sites that are in both the reference and the study after QC. We do not add back sites that failed earlier checks. We will prune the sites again later, after we define the final cohort.

### You need

The saved state from step 4.6, and the reference subset supplied at step 0.5.

### Command

```{r s5-2}
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
study_sites <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), ".pvar"))
reference_sites <- guided_table(paste0(reference, ".pvar"))
common <- sort(intersect(study_sites$ID, reference_sites$ID))
guided_list(common, guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt"))
stopifnot(length(common) == 48614L)
cat(length(common), "shared autosomal sites kept\n")
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "5.2", guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt"), parent = "4.6")
```

## 5.3 Match build, position and alleles {#step-5-3}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "All 48,614 shared IDs agree on chromosome, GRCh38 position and allele pair."} -->
### What we do

Check that the shared variants are really the same variants in both files, before the projection.

### Why

Two variants with the same [rsID](../docs/glossary.md#rsid) (a public name for a variant) are not always the same variant. For each shared variant, check four things: the genome build, the chromosome, the position and the pair of [alleles](../docs/glossary.md#allele). In step 4.5 the array-style names were replaced by IDs made of position and alleles.

If two files list the same two alleles in a different order, the variant is still compatible. If the allele pair differs, or the DNA strand is not resolved, we cannot accept the match without checking. The projection uses the named allele in each weight. It does not use the order of rows in the two files.

### You need

The list of common sites from step 5.2, and the two variant tables (the `.pvar` files) of the study and the reference.

### Command

```{r s5-3}
common <- readLines(guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), ".pvar"))
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
ref <- guided_table(paste0(reference, ".pvar"))
a <- match(common, study$ID); b <- match(common, ref$ID)
pair <- function(a, b) ifelse(a < b, paste0(a, b), paste0(b, a))
stopifnot(all(sub("^chr", "", study$CHROM[a]) == sub("^chr", "", ref$CHROM[b])),
  all(study$POS[a] == ref$POS[b]), all(pair(study$REF[a], study$ALT[a]) == pair(ref$REF[b], ref$ALT[b])))
cat("All", length(common), "shared sites agree on chromosome, position and alleles\n")
```

## 5.4 Reference PCA and study projection {#step-5-4}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "The study projection contains 1,844 samples."} -->
### What we do

Calculate the PCs in the reference only. Then place the reference samples and the study samples on the same axes.

### Why

If we ran one PCA on reference and study together, a much larger study group could pull the axes towards itself. So we fix the axes on the reference first. Placing new samples on fixed axes is called [projection](../docs/glossary.md#projection).

Each site has an allele weight (called a loading), which says how much that allele contributes to a PC. The score of a person is the sum of these weights over the alleles the person carries. The reference and the study scores must use the same allele frequencies, the same weights and the same standardisation. Standardisation means rescaling each genotype by the allele frequency, so that common and rare alleles count fairly. The scale and the sign (plus or minus) of a PC are arbitrary. Compare patterns only when both sets of scores use the same scale.

The weight file names the counted allele in a column called [A1](../docs/glossary.md#a1). We switch off mean imputation. This means a missing call is not replaced by the average, so the missing calls stay visible in the score.

### You need

The checked shared sites from step 5.3, and the full saved state from step 4.6.

### Command

```{r s5-4}
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
common <- guided_path(cfg, "5.2", "common.txt")
fit <- guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "reference")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", reference, "--extract", common, "--freq", "--pca", "10", "allele-wts", "--out", fit))
weights <- guided_table(paste0(fit, ".eigenvec.allele"))
id_column <- match("ID", names(weights)); allele_column <- match("A1", names(weights))
first_pc <- match("PC1", names(weights))
score <- c("--read-freq", paste0(fit, ".afreq"), "--score", paste0(fit, ".eigenvec.allele"),
  id_column, allele_column, "header-read", "no-mean-imputation", "variance-standardize",
  "--score-col-nums", paste0(first_pc, "-", first_pc + 9L))
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", reference, "--extract", common, score, "--out", guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores")))
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), "--extract", common, score, "--out", guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores")))
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "5.4", c(paste0(fit, c(".afreq", ".eigenvec", ".eigenval", ".eigenvec.allele")), paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"), paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore")), parent = "5.2")
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile data/course/pca_reference/ref1000g_grch38 --extract results/guided/s5-2_common.txt --freq --pca 10 allele-wts --out results/guided/s5-4_reference --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile data/course/pca_reference/ref1000g_grch38 --extract results/guided/s5-2_common.txt --read-freq results/guided/s5-4_reference.afreq --score results/guided/s5-4_reference.eigenvec.allele 2 5 header-read no-mean-imputation variance-standardize --score-col-nums 6-15 --out results/guided/s5-4_ref_scores --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s4-6_state --extract results/guided/s5-2_common.txt --read-freq results/guided/s5-4_reference.afreq --score results/guided/s5-4_reference.eigenvec.allele 2 5 header-read no-mean-imputation variance-standardize --score-col-nums 6-15 --out results/guided/s5-4_study_scores --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--extract` keeps only the checked shared sites. `--freq` writes the allele frequencies of the reference. `--pca 10 allele-wts` computes ten axes and saves the allele weights. `--read-freq` gives the same frequencies to both projections. `--score` names the weight file and the columns that hold the variant ID and the A1 allele (columns 2 and 5 here, counted from one). `header-read` tells PLINK to use the header line of the weight file. `no-mean-imputation` stops PLINK replacing missing calls with the average. `variance-standardize` scales the genotypes with the allele frequencies. `--score-col-nums 6-15` selects PC1 to PC10. The R command finds these column numbers from the real header line. `--pfile` reads the named genotype files in PLINK 2 format. `--out` sets the name of the output files. `--threads 2` limits the number of worker threads. `--memory 2048` sets the working memory to 2048 MiB.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Reference eigenvectors and eigenvalues, allele weights, and two `.sscore` files (score tables) with the columns PC1_AVG to PC10_AVG. The study projection contains 1,844 samples.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks and the expected counts passed on Windows.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error message. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### Quick check

Why must the study projection use the reference frequencies, and not recalculate the standardisation from the study alone?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Otherwise the two sets of scores would not share the same coordinate system.

</details>

### Files created

`s5-4_reference.*`, `s5-4_ref_scores.sscore`, `s5-4_study_scores.sscore` and logs.

<details><summary>Under the hood & literature</summary>

**What the tool computes.** `--pca 10 allele-wts` finds the top ten principal components of the reference genotypes after each variant is shifted to mean 0 and scaled to variance 1 with its allele frequency. The `.eigenvec.allele` file has one line per allele. After the variant ID and `A1`, each `PC` column is the weight of that allele on that component. `--score` then gives each person the average of weight times standardised genotype over the shared alleles. The `_AVG` columns are averages, so their scale differs from the `.eigenvec` file. Use the projected scores for both groups.

**Why these values.** Ten components is PLINK's default and a course convention. Step 5.7 fixes how many enter the model. `--read-freq` gives both groups the same frequencies. `no-mean-imputation` leaves missing calls out of the average.

**Pitfalls.** Projected study samples shrink towards the origin, and the bias grows from PC5 onwards, so read distances on later PCs with care. An allele that does not match by name contributes nothing, so the score silently uses fewer sites. At an A/T or C/G site, a strand flip keeps the name but reverses the meaning and flips the sign of its contribution. This is why the shared sites are checked at step 5.3. A person from an ancestry absent from the reference tends to land near the closest reference group. The spelling `variance-standardize` is American; the course text says standardise.

**References**

1. Patterson N et al. (2006) Population structure and eigenanalysis. PLoS Genet 2:e190. PMID 17194218.
2. Price AL et al. (2006) Principal components analysis corrects for stratification in genome-wide association studies. Nat Genet 38:904-909. PMID 16862161.
3. Privé F et al. (2020) Efficient toolkit implementing best practices for principal component analysis of population genetic data. Bioinformatics 36:4449-4457. PMID 32415959.
4. The 1000 Genomes Project Consortium (2015) A global reference for human genetic variation. Nature 526:68-74. PMID 26432245.

</details>

## 5.5 Plot the reference and projected study {#step-5-5}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "A labelled plot of the reference with the projected study."} -->
### What we do

Draw a plot of the first two reference axes. Each reference group has its own label and symbol, and the study samples are added on top.

### Why

A plot of two PCs helps us see large differences between samples. Later PCs can show patterns that PC1 and PC2 hide. A difference can also come from the genotyping platform, from missing data or from allele errors. The study points are projected scores. They are not a separate PCA. The groups use symbols as well as colour, so the plot stays readable without colour.

### You need

The score files from step 5.4, and the reference sample table.

### Command

```{r s5-5}
ref <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore"))
metadata <- guided_table(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38.psam"))
group <- metadata$SuperPop[match(ref$IID, metadata$IID)]
levels <- sort(unique(group)); code <- match(group, levels)
colours <- c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73", "#CC79A7", "#E69F00")
png(guided_path(cfg, "5.5", "reference_projection.png"), width = 1200, height = 850, res = 140)
plot(as.numeric(ref$PC1_AVG), as.numeric(ref$PC2_AVG), col = colours[code], pch = code,
  xlab = "Reference PC1 score", ylab = "Reference PC2 score", main = "GRCh38 reference and projected simulated study")
points(as.numeric(study$PC1_AVG), as.numeric(study$PC2_AVG), pch = 20, cex = 0.4, col = "#333333")
legend("topright", legend = c(levels, "Study projection"), col = c(colours[seq_along(levels)], "#333333"), pch = c(seq_along(levels), 20), cex = 0.8)
invisible(dev.off())
cat("The plot was saved to ", guided_path(cfg, "5.5", "reference_projection.png"), "\n", sep = "")
```

## 5.6 Define an ancestry-matched cohort {#step-5-6}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "33 remaining outlier records are excluded. 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants remain."} -->
### What we do

Apply a rule, fixed in advance, to the first four projected PCs. The rule flags samples that are more than six standard deviations from the European reference.

### Why

In this teaching design, the main analysis uses a cohort that broadly matches the European reference. The rule has three parts. First, take the European reference samples. For each of PC1 to PC4, calculate their mean and their [standard deviation](../docs/glossary.md#standard-deviation) (a measure of how spread out the values are). Second, convert each study score into a distance from that mean, counted in standard deviations. Third, flag a sample as an [outlier](../docs/glossary.md#outlier) if its largest distance, ignoring the sign, is above six.

This is a rule for this study only. It is not a general way to classify ancestry. Apply it before you look at any association results, and report who was excluded.

### You need

The reference and study scores from step 5.4, and the reference labels used in step 5.5.

### Command

```{r s5-6}
ref <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "ref_scores"), ".sscore"))
study <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.4", "study_scores"), ".sscore"))
metadata <- guided_table(file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38.psam"))
eur <- metadata$SuperPop[match(ref$IID, metadata$IID)] == "EUR"
columns <- paste0("PC", 1:4, "_AVG")
r <- sapply(ref[eur, columns, drop = FALSE], as.numeric)
s <- sapply(study[columns], as.numeric)
centre <- colMeans(r)
spread <- sqrt(colMeans(sweep(r, 2, centre, "-")^2))
z <- sweep(sweep(s, 2, centre, "-"), 2, spread, "/")
bad <- study$IID[apply(abs(z), 1, max) > 6]
remove <- guided_list(bad, guided_path(cfg, "5.6", "remove.txt"), TRUE)
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "4.6"), "--remove", remove, "--make-pgen", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "5.6")))
ops <- guided_replay_lists(cfg, "5.6", "4.6")
guided_register(cfg, "5.6", "5.4", 1811, 238513, operations = ops)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s4-6_state --remove results/guided/s5-6_remove.txt --make-pgen --out results/guided/s5-6_state --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

R applies the rule and writes the list of flagged sample IDs (IIDs). `--remove` takes out the samples on that list from the full study data. `--make-pgen` saves the retained cohort. `--pfile` reads the named genotype files in PLINK 2 format. `--out` sets the name of the output files. `--threads 2` limits the number of worker threads. `--memory 2048` sets the working memory to 2048 MiB.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

33 remaining outlier records are excluded. 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants remain. Some of the simulated outliers were already removed in earlier QC steps. So 33 is not the total number of outliers in the original data.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks and the expected counts passed on Windows.

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error message. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

### What this check can reveal

Large differences in ancestry compared with the reference, and possible technical outliers. A mismatch needs a review and a written study design. It does not mean that the excluded people are unsuitable in general.

### Quick check

Why does the rule use four PCs and not only the two shown in the plot?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

A difference that is weak or invisible on the first two axes can appear on later axes.

</details>

### Files created

`s5-6_remove.txt`, `s5-6_state.*` and replay metadata.

## 5.7 Cohort PCs and how many to include {#step-5-7}


<!-- step_meta: {"success_line": "Ten cohort PCs, a scree plot and a complete saved state for step 5.7 with 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants."} -->
### What we do

Calculate new PCs in the retained study cohort, look at the eigenvalues and save the full state.

### Why

The reference axes describe broad differences between world regions. PCs calculated inside the cohort can capture finer differences that matter for association. We prune the sites again, because the cohort has changed. We keep only common sites, which means a [minor allele frequency](../docs/glossary.md#maf) (MAF, the frequency of the rarer allele) of at least 0.05.

An [eigenvalue](../docs/glossary.md#eigenvalue) measures how much variation one PC explains. A [scree plot](../docs/glossary.md#scree-plot) shows the eigenvalues in order, from the largest to the smallest.

The course fixes the number of PCs at ten for the main model. We do not choose the number to get attractive p-values. Too few PCs can leave confounding in the results. Too many PCs can reduce the precision of the estimates. In module 7 we compare other numbers of PCs as a sensitivity check. We do not use that check to search for the most significant result.

### You need

The retained cohort from step 5.6, and the list of GRCh38 long-range LD regions to exclude.

### Command

```{r s5-7}
regions <- guided_high_ld(cfg)
prune <- guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "prune")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.6"), "--chr", "1-22", "--maf", "0.05", "--exclude", "bed1", regions,
  "--indep-pairwise", "200kb", "0.2", "--out", prune))
report <- guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "pca")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.6"), "--extract", paste0(prune, ".prune.in"), "--pca", "10", "--out", report))
eigenvalues <- scan(paste0(report, ".eigenval"), quiet = TRUE)
png(guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "scree.png"), width = 1000, height = 700, res = 130)
plot(seq_along(eigenvalues), eigenvalues, type = "b", pch = 16, xlab = "PC number", ylab = "Eigenvalue", main = "Retained cohort: first ten PCs")
invisible(dev.off())
cat("The plot was saved to ", guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "scree.png"), "\n", sep = "")
guided_snapshot(cfg, "5.7", guided_path(cfg, "5.6"), 1811, 238513, parent = "5.6")
file.copy(paste0(report, c(".eigenvec", ".eigenval")), file.path(cfg$out, "checkpoints", "5.7"), overwrite = TRUE)
check_step("5.7", data_dir = cfg$out, work_dir = cfg$out)
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-6_state --chr 1-22 --maf 0.05 --exclude bed1 results/guided/s3-4_high_ld.bed1 --indep-pairwise 200kb 0.2 --out results/guided/s5-7_prune --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-6_state --extract results/guided/s5-7_prune.prune.in --pca 10 --out results/guided/s5-7_pca --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--maf 0.05` keeps only common sites for the pruning. `--chr 1-22` keeps only autosomal sites. `--exclude bed1` skips the long-range LD regions listed in a one-based BED file. `--indep-pairwise 200kb 0.2` writes the list of sites left after pruning, using windows of 200 kb and an r^2 limit of 0.2. `--extract` uses that list only for the PCA. `--pca 10` computes the ten cohort eigenvectors. `--pfile` reads the named genotype files in PLINK 2 format. `--out` sets the name of the output files. `--threads 2` limits the number of worker threads. `--memory 2048` sets the working memory to 2048 MiB.

<details><summary>Show the expected result</summary>

Ten cohort PCs, a scree plot and a complete saved state for step 5.7 with 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants. The first cohort eigenvalue is about 14. The signs of the eigenvectors can differ on your computer. This does not change how the PCs adjust the association. R saves the picture as a PNG file and prints its path. It does not show the picture in the console. To see it, open the file from the Files pane of RStudio (click the file name, then choose "View File").

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks and the expected counts passed on Windows.

```{r s5-7_expected_figure, echo=FALSE, fig.alt="The first cohort eigenvalue is much larger than the subsequent nine; ten PCs are prespecified for association."}
if (requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE) && knitr::is_html_output()) {
  knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "scree.png"), winslash = "/", mustWork = FALSE), rel_path = FALSE)
}
```

</details>

<details><summary>If something goes wrong</summary>

Stop at the first error message. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).

</details>

## Module 5 recap {#module-5-recap}

- You compared the study with a GRCh38 reference subset of 1,062 samples.
- You kept 48,614 shared sites, and all of them matched on chromosome, position and alleles.
- You placed 1,844 study samples on the reference axes and drew the plot.
- You applied the six-standard-deviation rule and excluded 33 outlier records.
- 1,811 samples and 238,513 variants remain, with ten cohort PCs ready for the association model.

**Next:** module 6, where you run the association test and use these PCs as covariates.
